title: The Biloxi White House engagement of 1932-34 and its terms
summary: DeDroit explains how Mr. Cobb let him leave for the White House hotel summers at $250 a week, and reflects on his hard work.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: What years were you at the pavilion about? Was it 32? According to your clippings there, I think it was. 32 to 34. Well, that's not, I think that was the years that you had there.

Well, those were my biggest years when I played in Biloxi, because I was that good at Walter White. I was like, Mr. Cobb used to keep us in the summertime just to have us in the winter. But when he found out that I wanted to go to the White House, he arranged it. In fact, Walter White came there one night with Joe Fulco, and I introduced him to Mr. Cobb. He said, Mr. Cobb, I'm trying to get Johnny every year to come home and play at the White House. He says, it's loyal to you, Mr. Cobb. Well, he says, I keep Johnny in the summertime, I don't make any money. And if Johnny wants to go to the White House, it'll be okay with me, providing he comes back Labor Day. So Walter White said, Mr. Cobb, Labor Day is our biggest day. It's the end of the season. It was the 14-week-end game to see. So Mr. Cobb considered that I should open up the day after Labor Day. So I didn't have to worry. I knew that I was going to play at the White House. I got room and board for my wife and I and my daughter. I got a beautiful room. I got 20% off of laundry. I got $250 a week to play three hours a night. No Sundays. You know that.

I had to build my dear I was lucky. I worked hard. I worked too hard. I wouldn't go through it again. And I'd wind up just the same. Well, that's not like it did you any harm, you know? No, no, I'm independent. You know what I mean? My wife and I, my sister's wife, we only had two years, and we made six trips already. We got a couple of them there. We'd travel and go see. And I'd go to shrine conventions, too.
